wisdom.opening: Dawn. A pot scrapes the courtyard wall. Your father is leaving before anyone can ask him for advice.
wisdom.scene:courtyard: The cooking fire is cold. One enormous pot is missing. Beyond the wall, Anansi’s footprints point toward the forest; someone has brushed leaves over them in a hurry.
wisdom.scene:market: A potter repairs a cracked water jar. “Your father asked whether a tree could keep a secret,” she says. “I told him trees have roots everywhere.” A cloth and a spare gourd lie beside her tools.
wisdom.scene:well: The bucket is full. Carrying water takes a moment, but a hot day in the forest can make that moment worthwhile.
wisdom.scene:trail: One track goes down to the river. The other climbs through thorns toward a high crossing. Anansi has taken the low path. Rain clouds are collecting behind the hills.
wisdom.scene:ridge: A fallen trunk spans the ravine. Rain has polished its bark. From here you can reach the grove without disturbing the ferry, if you can keep both hands free.
wisdom.scene:river: A ferryman struggles with a tangled mooring. Anansi has already crossed on stepping stones. Water darkens their edges. You can help, investigate the ford, or spend time finding another route.
wisdom.scene:ford: Three pale stones break the surface. The center one rocks under drifting branches. The far bank is close, but the color of water does not reveal its depth.
wisdom.scene:grove: Anansi is not here, but a branch trembles high above. A boy collecting fallen wood says he heard a pot arguing with itself. He offers to show you the tree if you help carry his bundle.
wisdom.scene:tree: Your father clings to the trunk. The pot hangs in front of his knees. “Go home,” he says. “This is a matter for someone who knows everything.” The cord gives a small, sharp creak.
wisdom.scene:knot: You can show Anansi how to carry the load. Arrange three steps: make a loop, put the weight behind the carrier, then tighten. The order matters; tightening first leaves no space for the pot.
wisdom.scene:ledge: The pot rests on a branch between you. A hairline crack runs beneath its wax. Anansi reaches for it, then hesitates. You have one clear moment to decide what you are trying to save.
wisdom.scene:pot: A hundred contradictory answers press against the clay. Some are warnings. Some are jokes. One voice keeps asking who decided that knowing a thing meant owning it.
wisdom.scene:council: The ferryman, potter, and wood-gatherer have followed the sound. Anansi sets the pot in the middle. Nobody asks him to be right. They ask what he wants to do next.
wisdom.scene:squall: Rain crashes through the canopy. The path becomes a stream. You have to protect your footing before you can return to what you were doing.
wisdom.ending:shared: The seal opens without a crack. Each person hears an answer in a voice they recognize. Anansi is still a storyteller; now he can also ask questions. You leave the empty pot in the grove, where anyone can sit beside it.
wisdom.ending:keeper: Anansi breaks the newer seal himself. The pot stays in his courtyard, but its door stays open. You write one condition beside it: a keeper must listen as often as they speak. It is an imperfect arrangement, with room to change.
wisdom.ending:scattered: The clay gives way, by accident or invitation. Wisdom scatters beyond the grove. Nobody receives all of it, and nobody can gather it all again. Later you hear a child tell a story your father never knew. You carry that news home.
wisdom.ending:storyteller: Instead of taking an answer out, Anansi tells one in: the child’s story from another telling. The voices in the clay go quiet to listen. One by one, people around the circle add a story of their own. By midnight the pot holds more than it did at dawn, and nobody owns any of it. Anansi is still the cleverest person in the grove. Now he is also its best listener.

tide.opening: The sea pulls away from the shore. Something trapped in a bright loop of line moves beneath a rock.
tide.scene:shore: A sea turtle has caught its flipper in discarded fishing line. Your boat sits above the wet sand. A net knife rests beside it. The water is returning, one small pool at a time.
tide.scene:pools: The turtle turns back. “You gave me time,” it says. “Would you like to see where ours begins?” It nudges a small shell toward you. Behind it, the sea opens into a green road.
tide.scene:channel: Silver fish drift past your shoulder. The road forks around a column of bubbles. A chain of old bells marks the quiet passage; a bright open tunnel promises a faster descent.
tide.scene:gate: A roof of deep red tiles hangs against the green water. Otohime waits at the gate. “Welcome, Urashima,” she says. “Ask for what you need. Guests who never ask sometimes forget to leave.”
tide.scene:hall: Spring rain touches one window. Summer insects tick against another. Leaves turn at the third; snow gathers at the fourth. The feast looks freshly set, but something about the bowls is wrong.
tide.scene:garden: Four carved rings regulate the current. An inscription gives their order: spring rain feeds summer growth; autumn releases it; winter lets it rest. Set the rings in that order to still the water around the archive.
tide.scene:stillwater: In this corridor the palace becomes transparent. Years slide past outside like schools of fish. The turtle cannot choose which one carries you home without a chart.
tide.scene:archive: The archivist has no books. Each shelf holds a bottle of seawater from a particular morning. “The princess offers a box when guests leave,” the archivist says. “It keeps a debt of time. Ask what happens when it opens.”
tide.scene:feast: Otohime asks about the people on your shore. When you describe them, she listens carefully. “I can give you a place here,” she says. “I cannot promise your home will wait.”
tide.scene:promise: “Your shore will have changed,” Otohime says. “With this chart, I can limit the years that pass. I will not hide the cost in a gift.” The turtle waits beside the marked current.
tide.scene:gift: Otohime places the box in your hands. “Keep it closed until you know what it holds.” Its cord has no knot you recognize. The shell against your chest sounds like a distant harbor bell.
tide.scene:return: From below, your coast is a thin silver line. The turtle asks for a direction. It will follow your chart, your earlier promise, a morning you can name, or simply the strongest current. Those are different journeys.
tide.scene:newShore: The mountain is where it was. The houses are not. A child on the beach recognizes your boat only from a story. You still have to decide what to carry into this changed world.
tide.scene:homeSea: The palace is beautiful. Beyond it, people mend roofs, argue over moorings, and need hands to help. A life here would be a life of work and friendship, not a never-ending feast.
tide.scene:surge: Water rushes across the corridor. A gate begins to turn. You must anchor yourself, cut a jam, swim for it, or wait for the current to spend its force.
tide.ending:home: You cannot recover every morning you missed. But the marked current brings you to a shore close enough to recognize and a harbor where your story can be checked. You begin with names, then with a meal. Home is something you can build again.
tide.ending:sea: You take a room above the lower harbor. Some days you miss the smell of land after rain. Some days you repair a boat beside someone who has never seen a tree. Otohime still visits. Your choice becomes an ordinary, extraordinary life.
tide.ending:century: The names you knew have become stories. Whether you release the years or keep carrying them, your past cannot be restored by a box. The child on the shore asks what really happened. You sit on an overturned boat and begin telling it.
tide.ending:door: The turtle carries the unopened box back to Otohime with a message: you will come down at every spring low tide, and she is welcome to come up. The years stay where they are, held like water behind a harbor wall, neither spent nor wasted. On the shore, the child asks what really happened. This time you can say: it is still happening.

orchestra.opening: The farm gate falls shut behind you. Ahead is the road to Bremen. For the first time in years, no one is telling you what to carry.
orchestra.scene:road: You are an old donkey with a strong back and a voice no one has thought to ask about. A dog lies in the shade ahead. Beside the milestone, a traveler has left bread and an old harness bell.
orchestra.scene:dog: The dog has run from a house that no longer wanted him. “I can still keep watch,” he says. “I simply cannot run all day.” A song could use a steady beat as much as a loud voice.
orchestra.scene:orchard: A cat sits on the wall above a loop of loose cord. She has left a house where warmth had become conditional on catching mice. “What are you two doing?” she asks. “You walk as if it was your idea.”
orchestra.scene:rooster: A rooster announces tomorrow as if volume could guarantee it. He has heard the cook planning supper. “Come with us,” you can say. But he wants to know who decides what the group sings.
orchestra.scene:wood: Bremen is too far for tonight. From a high branch, the rooster sees a light. The dog smells food, then a guard’s boots. A house in the clearing may be shelter, but someone is already using it.
orchestra.scene:clearing: Through the window you see a feast and sacks marked with names from nearby farms. A thief writes in a ledger. The cat can reach the pantry. The dog can watch the gate. You can choose how this becomes your problem.
orchestra.scene:pantry: The cat returns with a route to the ledger. “I can take it,” she says, “but the floorboards will tell on me. One distraction, please.” The dog waits for your signal.
orchestra.scene:witness: A miller has followed a stolen cart here. She can identify the sacks. “I cannot walk into that room alone,” she says. “But I can carry a message if you can get everyone out.”
orchestra.scene:gate: The guard has just passed the gate. If you studied the tracks, you know the next stop. Otherwise you can spend a turn observing, use a remote bell, or accept the risk of an early entrance.
orchestra.scene:rehearsal: Build the sound from the ground up. Your low bray is the foundation. The dog adds a beat, the cat a high phrase, and the rooster ends above everyone. Rehearse that order before you attempt it at the window.
orchestra.scene:window: The thieves are arguing about the missing lookout. You can launch a rehearsed entrance, improvise a wall of sound, or back away with what you know. The dog is ready by the door.
orchestra.scene:hearth: The room is yours for the moment. The sacks still belong to their owners. Outside, the thieves are beginning to wonder whether the terrible creature was only noise. You need a plan for their return.
orchestra.scene:lastWatch: One thief has come back to test the house. The dog needs a clear signal, the cat needs space, and the rooster needs to wait for the right moment. Harmony can hold this room. Evidence can carry you out of it.
orchestra.scene:escape: The road to town begins beyond the orchard. You can bring a witness and proof, or leave the house behind and keep the ensemble moving. The night has changed you; it does not have to finish you.
orchestra.scene:patrol: The lookout returns early. Your companions freeze. You need to send the boots away, hold perfectly still, or move everyone to new cover.
orchestra.ending:home: The returning thief hears one voice at the door, another at the hearth, and two more above him. He flees. In the morning you return the sacks and invite their owners to a concert. You may still reach Bremen one day. For now, there is room around this fire.
orchestra.ending:case: The ledger has dates. The miller has names. You have four accounts that agree where it matters and disagree everywhere else. By noon the stolen goods are being returned. The town asks whether its new investigators also take concert bookings.
orchestra.ending:road: You meet beyond the orchard as promised. The house remains behind you, with all its unfinished business. The cat says your entrance was terrible. The rooster says the ending needs work. The dog counts four shadows on the road. You have another day to practice.
orchestra.ending:bremen: In the old telling the four musicians never reach Bremen. This time you walk in at dawn: a donkey, a dog, a cat, a rooster, a miller, and a ledger. The magistrate reads the dates. The miller names the sacks. By evening the town has hired its first municipal orchestra, on the condition that it never rehearses before breakfast.

olives.opening: Morning in Baghdad. At an inn by the Tigris, a merchant home from seven years of travel is staring at a plate of olives as if they had insulted him.
olives.scene:inn: Ali Cogia sits among plates of emptied olives like a man at his own funeral. Mecca, Cairo, Damascus, India: seven years of travel, and he came home to a jar with nothing under the olives. He does not notice you until you sit down.
olives.scene:street: Awnings, scales, and arguments. Everyone has heard about Ali Cogia and the cadi’s verdict. Half the street thinks Ali is a liar; the other half thinks his friend is. Nobody has thought to check.
olives.scene:shop: Ali’s old friend sells cloth and lamp oil. He greets you warmly, as he greets everyone. Behind him, on a high shelf, a ring in the dust marks where the jar stood for seven years.
olives.scene:house: The merchant’s wife is beating a rug as if it had personally wronged her. She sees you glance toward the shop and stops, mid-swing.
olives.scene:olives: Barrels of green and black olives, crocks of brine, and two old dealers who sit side by side and disagree about everything except olives.
olives.scene:court: The cadi is hearing a dispute about a goat. A clerk recognizes Ali’s name and snorts. “Dismissed. No witnesses, and the friend swore an oath. Next.”
olives.scene:fountain: A dozen children are already playing at the case, badly. Nobody wants to be Ali Cogia, everyone wants to be the cadi, and one boy has declared himself the caliph and is refusing to come down from the fountain.
olives.scene:casting: Four parts, four children, and very strong feelings. Ali Cogia must be wronged, the merchant must be a convincing villain, the olive dealers must agree, and the officer must be heard across the whole courtyard.
olives.scene:trial: Twelve children, one moon, and a cushion for the cadi’s seat. Lamps on the wall, an audience on the roof. In the dark corner by the gate, three grown men in plain cloaks stand very still.
olives.scene:trialJar: Ali Cogia (or whoever is playing him) pleads his case. The merchant (or whoever is playing him) swears he never touched the jar. Before any oath, a careful cadi examines the evidence.
olives.scene:trialDealers: Spoons, olives, an audience on the roof, and a cadi who must now decide. The merchant’s oath is waiting. So is the truth, if you can make it speak louder than him.
olives.scene:corner: The tallest stranger tastes an olive and does not hurry. His companions do not look at him the way companions look at each other. They look at him the way a street looks at a procession.
olives.scene:alley: The merchant catches up with you where the awnings end. He crouches to your height, smiling. “You are a clever child. Clever children should have sweets, not trouble.” He presses a gold piece into your palm.
olives.ending:verdict: Next morning the caliph hears Ali Cogia’s petition and does exactly what the courtyard did: he sends for olive dealers. This year’s harvest, they say. The merchant’s oath collapses; the gold is dug up from under his shop floor and returned to the last piece, and he pays a fine to the poor of the quarter. Ali Cogia buys new olives. He does not ask anyone to keep them.
olives.ending:mercy: Before any verdict, the merchant confesses: the craving, the lamp, the rotten olives, the gold, the long month of lying. He returns every piece. Ali Cogia does not embrace him, but he does not leave Baghdad either. A year later the two men are seen arguing in the market about the price of lamp oil, which everyone agrees is a good sign.
olives.ending:dismissed: The game ends in a shrug. Tomorrow the caliph, without a better method, accepts the same oath the cadi did. Ali Cogia leaves Baghdad again, this time with nothing to leave behind. Months later you taste a fresh olive and understand what you failed to ask.
olives.ending:caliph: The courtyard goes silent: Harun al-Rashid has been watching your game. “Tomorrow,” he says, “you will sit beside me while I hear this case, and you will ask the questions.” In the morning you do. The merchant does not swear. The gold comes back from under his floor. Ali Cogia and his old friend leave the palace by different doors, but both of them stop to thank the child who would not take an oath for an answer.
